admirablePeople.title: Who Do You Admire?
admirablePeople.description: Add 3–5 people: someone you know, a public figure, or a historical figure. Under each, list the qualities you admire in them.
admirablePeople.why: The qualities you admire in others usually reflect what matters to you. They are easier to name than your values when asked directly.
admirablePeople.qualityPlaceholder: E.g. tells the truth even when it's hard

coreValues.title: What Values Lie Behind These Qualities?
coreValues.description: Group similar qualities and name what they share, e.g. honesty or courage. Enter each value in its own field.
coreValues.why: A value is a direction you choose, not a box to tick. Once it has a name, it is easier to check whether your choices move you that way.

start.title: Map your values
start.description: You'll go from a long list of values to a map: which are central, which support them, where they clash, and in which life areas they matter.
start.sortBody: Move each value into a rough importance group. Fast, imperfect choices are enough.
start.rankBody: Narrow the list to 5-10 values and put them in a clear order.
start.conflictsBody: Capture places where two good values pull in different directions.
start.areasBody: Assign values to life areas without rating alignment or planning actions.

sort.title: Sort the value cards
sort.description: Drag each card from the list below into the column that shows how much it matters to you today. Decide quickly.
sort.why: Quick choices bypass what you think you should value and show what actually matters. Sorting forces trade-offs, because not everything can be most important.

narrow.title: Choose 5–10 values
narrow.description: Click the ones that should go into your ranking. Only values from Most important and Very important are shown here.
narrow.why: A short list is one you can remember and actually use when deciding. When thirty values are all important, none of them points the way.
narrow.tooFewCandidates: You have fewer than 5 high-priority values. Go back to sorting and mark a few more as Most important or Very important.
narrow.selectionHint: Selected: {count}. Choose at least 5 and at most 10.

rank.title: Rank your selected values
rank.description: Drag the cards or use the arrows. Put on top what you'd choose when two values collide. The top three are your core values.
rank.why: A ranking shows what comes first when you can't have everything. Your top three go into your profile as the core the assistant draws on.

meaning.title: Define what they mean to you
meaning.description: Describe in your own words what each value looks like in your everyday life. The top three (*) are required; the rest are optional.
meaning.why: The same word means different things to different people. Your own definition turns a label into something you can recognise in how you live.

conflicts.title: Name value tensions
conflicts.description: When two important values pull you in different directions (e.g. freedom and security), mark them and describe when it happens. Optional.
conflicts.why: A tension between values isn't a flaw; it's where the hard decisions are. Knowing it lets you choose deliberately instead of being pulled back and forth.
conflicts.itemQuestion: Does {value} often compete with another value?
conflicts.notePlaceholder: E.g. when I have to choose between…

areas.title: Assign values to life areas
areas.description: For each area, pick the values that matter there and click Add. They can differ from your ranking.
areas.why: Different things can matter at work, in relationships or in health. Linking values to areas tells you what to steer by in each part of life.
areas.empty: No active life areas are available. You can skip this step or create areas first.
areas.tensionQuestion: Is there a value tension in this area?

summary.title: Review your value map
summary.description: Check the hierarchy and context before saving.
summary.notesPlaceholder: Any additional notes about this map...

shadowBeliefs.title: Shadow Beliefs
shadowBeliefs.description: Shadow beliefs are deep, often unexamined assumptions that can quietly undermine your decisions and actions. This exercise helps you notice them — not to judge yourself, but to build awareness.

beliefs.title: Which of these beliefs do you recognize in yourself?
beliefs.description: Select any that feel familiar, or add your own.
beliefs.customPlaceholder: E.g. I have to earn my rest
beliefs.examineHint: For each belief, you can look at the evidence and search for a truer version. These fields are optional.
beliefs.why: A belief sounds like a fact but usually rests on a few selected moments. Weighing evidence for and against shows the fuller picture and a version closer to the truth.
beliefs.reframePlaceholder: Closer to the truth is that…

commonBeliefs.somethingWrong: There is something wrong with me
commonBeliefs.dontDeserve: I don't deserve what I want

doEverythingMyself.m: I have to do everything myself
doEverythingMyself.f: I have to do everything myself

advice.title: Advice You Give Others
advice.description: Write down advice you often give others, and mark whether you follow it yourself.
advice.why: A gap between what you advise others and what you allow yourself often points to a hidden belief, e.g. that stricter rules apply to you.
advice.placeholder: E.g. Take a break, nothing will fall apart
advice.blockerLabel: What stops you from applying it to yourself?
advice.blockerPlaceholder: Maybe I believe that in my case…

reflectionPlaceholder.m: Note what you noticed during this exercise...
reflectionPlaceholder.f: Note what you noticed during this exercise...

curiosities.title: What Are You Curious About?
curiosities.description: List five things you're genuinely curious about. Don't filter — include anything that draws your attention.
curiosities.why: Curiosity doesn't need to be forced. A purpose built on what already draws you in is easier to sustain for years.

intersection.title: What Connects Your Curiosities?
intersection.description: Look for a theme that runs through all or most of them. Describe it in a sentence or two.
intersection.why: The thread running through several interests says more than any one of them. It's where you're most likely to find a purpose that won't bore you.

problems.title: Which Problems Do You Want to Help Solve?
problems.description: List up to five big problems (in the world, among people, in your field) connected to your common thread.
problems.why: Curiosity gives you energy; a problem gives you direction. A purpose that serves something beyond you keeps its meaning on harder days too.

purpose.title: Your Purpose Statement
purpose.description: Combine your common thread with one of the problems in a single sentence. It's a draft: live with it for 2–3 months and refine it.
purpose.why: One sentence is easy to remember and test decisions against: does this move me closer? Treating it as a draft takes off the pressure to find the one true purpose right away.
purpose.placeholder: My purpose is to help… so that…
purpose.reflectionPlaceholder: E.g. what doesn't quite fit yet…

intro.title: Thought Record
intro.description: A thought record helps you examine and restructure negative thinking patterns. You'll work through a structured process based on Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT).
intro.howItWorksDescription: By examining the evidence for and against your automatic thoughts, you can develop more balanced perspectives and reduce emotional distress.

situation.title: Describe the situation
situation.description: Write what happened: where, when, who was there, what was said. Just the facts, the way a camera would record it.
situation.why: Separating facts from interpretation is the core of a thought record. Thoughts and judgements get their own step, so here you keep only what could be checked.
situation.placeholder: e.g. At Tuesday's meeting my manager cut me off mid-sentence.

emotions.title: How are you feeling about this situation?
emotions.description: Select the emotions you feel and set how strong each one is (0–100%).
emotions.why: This rating is your baseline. At the end you'll rate the same emotions again and see whether working with the thought changed anything.

thoughts.title: What thoughts went through your mind?
thoughts.description: Write down the thoughts that came up in this situation, one per field. Use the flame icon to mark the “hot thought”: the one behind the strongest emotion.
thoughts.why: Emotions usually come less from the situation itself than from how we read it. Next you'll test only the hot thought, because it drives most of what you feel.
thoughts.placeholder: e.g. Everyone will think I can't cope.

evidenceFor.title: What evidence supports this thought?
evidenceFor.description: List the facts that support this thought, one per field. What counts is what happened, not how you feel.
evidenceFor.why: Giving the “for” side a fair hearing keeps the next steps from turning into forced self-persuasion. A conclusion that weighs both sides is easier to accept.
evidenceFor.placeholder: e.g. My manager sent my report back for revisions twice.

evidenceAgainst.title: What evidence goes against this thought?
evidenceAgainst.description: List facts that don't fit it and other possible explanations for what happened. A useful question: what would a kind friend point out?
evidenceAgainst.why: Strong emotion narrows attention to whatever confirms the thought. Deliberately looking for counter-examples widens the picture.
evidenceAgainst.placeholder: e.g. Last month my manager praised my project.
evidenceAgainst.followUpPlaceholder: Nothing comes to mind... / Tell me more...

balancedThought.title: Write a balanced thought
balancedThought.description: Write one or two sentences that take the evidence on both sides into account. It doesn't have to be positive, just closer to the facts.
balancedThought.why: The aim isn't positive thinking but more accurate thinking. A thought you can genuinely believe eases emotions better than an affirmation.
balancedThought.placeholder: e.g. The report needed fixes, but I usually do a good job.
balancedThought.followUpPlaceholder: Can you try a different angle?

rerate.title: Re-rate your emotions now
rerate.description: Move the sliders to how strong these emotions are now. Your starting rating is shown alongside.
rerate.why: Comparing before and after shows how much of the distress depended on the thought. Even a small drop counts, and no change is useful information too.

learningIntro.title: What Are Cognitive Distortions?
learningIntro.description1: Cognitive distortions are automatic thinking patterns that distort reality. Everyone has them. Learning to recognise them is the first step to thinking more clearly.
learningIntro.description2: In this exercise you will learn 14 common cognitive distortions from CBT, popularised by David Burns, then check which ones you recognise in your own thinking.

selfCheck.title: Which of these do you recognise in your own thinking?
selfCheck.description: Click the ones that happen to you — you can pick several.
selfCheck.why: Everyone has a few favourite thinking traps. Once you know yours, it's easier to catch them in the moment they appear.
selfCheck.personalReflectionsDescription: Optional: for each one you picked, note a situation or thought where you see it in yourself.
selfCheck.personalExamplePlaceholder: When and how it shows up for you...

appliedThought.title: Examine a Thought
appliedThought.description: Enter one thought that's bothering you, word for word as it sounds in your head. You'll check whether a thinking trap (a distortion) is hiding in it.
appliedThought.why: Written down, a thought stops being an obvious truth and becomes something you can look at. The exact wording matters: distortions often sit in words like “always”, “nobody”, “must”.
appliedThought.placeholder: e.g. I'm definitely going to mess it all up again.

appliedDistortions.title: Spot the Distortions
appliedDistortions.description: Select the cards that fit this thought — there may be several. Then note for each one how you can tell.
appliedDistortions.why: Naming the trap creates distance: it is no longer “the truth about me” but a familiar habit of the mind. Pointing to the exact words sets up the reframe in the next step.
appliedDistortions.explanationPlaceholder: Which words or assumptions in the thought point to it...

appliedResults.title: Reframe the Thought
appliedResults.description: For each distortion, write how the thought would sound without it. The notes below are optional.
appliedResults.why: Naming a trap doesn't change the thought by itself. A version without the distortion gives you an alternative to return to when the old thought comes back.
appliedResults.reframePlaceholder: The thought without this trap, e.g. “This time it didn't work out, but…”
appliedResults.notesPlaceholder: Any other thoughts about this analysis...

capture.title: What's worrying you?
capture.description: Describe in your own words what you're worried might happen, in a sentence or a few.
capture.why: A worry kept in your head circles and grows. Written down, it becomes concrete and can be worked through step by step.
capture.emotionsDescription: Pick the emotion that most goes with this worry and rate its strength on the slider. You'll rate it again at the end.

classify.title: What kind of worry is this?
classify.description: Ask yourself: is this something happening now that you can influence, or a “what if” scenario?
classify.why: A real problem calls for action; a hypothetical worry calls for letting go. Mixing them up means trying to solve something that can't be solved.
classify.realProblemDescription: Something concrete you can actually do something about
classify.hypotheticalDescription: A "what if" scenario that may never happen

canAct.title: Can you take action right now?
canAct.description: Is there a concrete step you can take on this problem today?
canAct.yesDescription: There is something concrete I can do about this today
canAct.noDescription: I need to wait or schedule this for later

actionPlan.title: Plan Your Action
actionPlan.description: Write the very next step you can take — small and specific. Pick a date below.
actionPlan.why: A small step with a date turns circling thoughts into action. Even partial progress eases the sense of helplessness.
actionPlan.createCommitment: Create a Commitment from this action

schedule.title: Schedule It
schedule.description: You can't act right now, but you can decide when you'll deal with it. Write the first step and pick a date below.
schedule.why: Once a matter has a set date, it no longer needs to circle in your head — your mind knows it won't be forgotten.

encouragement.m: You've acknowledged the problem and scheduled a time to deal with it. For now, take a deep breath. You don't need to solve this in this moment.
encouragement.f: You've acknowledged the problem and scheduled a time to deal with it. For now, take a deep breath. You don't need to solve this in this moment.

lettingGo.title: Set This Worry Aside
lettingGo.description: This worry is about something that hasn't happened and may never happen. It doesn't need solving — only setting aside for now.
lettingGo.why: The mind is wired to scan for threats, even imagined ones, so worries like this are normal. What helps is changing how you relate to them, not analysing them further.
lettingGo.choosePrompt: Try one of these techniques for a minute, then click it to move on:

leavesOnStream.name: Leaves on a Stream
leavesOnStream.description: Visualize placing the worry on a leaf and watching it float gently down a stream, away from you.

refocus.name: Refocus
refocus.description: Gently redirect your attention to what you are doing right now. Notice five things you can see around you.

worryTime.name: Worry Time
worryTime.description: Note this worry for a scheduled 15-minute worry window later today. You have permission to set it aside until then.

acceptance.name: Acceptance
acceptance.description: Acknowledge the uncertainty without fighting it. You don't have to resolve every unknown right now.

recheck.title: How are you feeling now?
recheck.description: Take a moment to check in with yourself. Rate the same emotion again.

intro.title: Core Beliefs Exploration
intro.description: Core beliefs are the deepest thoughts we hold about ourselves, others, and the world. They form early in life and shape how we interpret everything that happens to us.
intro.techniqueDescription: By repeatedly asking "If that were true, what would it mean?", you can trace a surface thought down to the deeper belief underneath it.

startingThought.title: What thought do you want to explore?
startingThought.description: Enter a thought that has kept coming back lately — after a conversation, a mistake, or a difficult situation, for example.
startingThought.why: Everyday thoughts are a way into deeper beliefs. A thought that keeps returning and hurts usually leads closest to what lies underneath.
startingThought.placeholder: e.g. “I always mess things up” or “Nobody really cares about me”
startingThought.sourceLabel: Where does this thought come from? (optional)

downwardArrow.title: Go Beneath the Thought
downwardArrow.description: Answer the question below and add a layer, then ask the same about that answer. Stop when you reach a short statement about yourself, others, or the world.
downwardArrow.why: Each “what would that mean?” uncovers the assumption beneath the previous answer. Usually after 3–5 layers a short, general statement like “I am…” appears — that is the core belief.
downwardArrow.questionLabel: If that were true, what would it mean?

coreBelief.title: Your Core Belief
coreBelief.description: The field holds the last layer of the arrow. Edit it if needed so it reads as a short, general statement you've told yourself for a long time.
coreBelief.why: A core belief sounds like a general truth, not an opinion about one situation. Rating how strongly you believe it gives you a baseline to compare against at the end.

description.m: "I am unlovable", "I am incompetent", "I am worthless"
description.f: "I am unlovable", "I am incompetent", "I am worthless"

others.label: About Others
others.description: "People can't be trusted", "Others will always leave"

coreBelief.believabilityTitle: How much do you believe this right now?

evidenceFor.title: What supports this belief?
evidenceFor.description: List the experiences and facts it rests on, one per field.
evidenceFor.why: Core beliefs have their origins and often once made sense. Acknowledging what they rest on keeps the next step honest rather than a fight with yourself.
evidenceFor.placeholder: e.g. As a child I was rarely praised.

evidenceAgainst.title: What goes against this belief?
evidenceAgainst.description: List experiences that don't fit it — including small ones and ones you usually overlook.
evidenceAgainst.why: A strong belief works like a filter: it notices what confirms it and screens out the rest. Deliberately looking for exceptions weakens that filter.
evidenceAgainst.placeholder: e.g. A friend called when I was having a hard time.

alternative.title: Write a more balanced belief
alternative.description: Based on the evidence on both sides, write a statement closer to the truth than the old one. It doesn't have to be positive, just realistic.
alternative.why: The old belief won't vanish at once. A new, realistic statement gives you an alternative to strengthen over time — for example in the Positive Data Log.
alternative.placeholder: e.g. I make mistakes sometimes, but many things go well for me.
alternative.followUpPlaceholder: Can you try a different angle?
alternative.rerateTitle: How much do you believe each one now?

intro.title: Compassionate Letter

description.m: Self-compassion means treating yourself with the same kindness you'd show a good friend. When we struggle, we often become our own harshest critic. This exercise helps you respond to difficult moments with warmth instead of judgment.
description.f: Self-compassion means treating yourself with the same kindness you'd show a good friend. When we struggle, we often become our own harshest critic. This exercise helps you respond to difficult moments with warmth instead of judgment.

intro.selfKindnessDescription: Being warm toward yourself when you suffer, rather than ignoring your pain or punishing yourself.
intro.commonHumanityDescription: Recognizing that suffering and personal inadequacy are part of the shared human experience.
intro.mindfulnessDescription: Holding painful thoughts and feelings in balanced awareness, rather than over-identifying with them.

situation.title: What happened, or what are you struggling with?

description.m: Describe it as if telling a trusted friend. There's no need to analyze or judge — just say what's going on.
description.f: Describe it as if telling a trusted friend. There's no need to analyze or judge — just say what's going on.

situation.placeholder: Something happened that's been weighing on me...

emotions.title: How are you feeling?
emotions.description: Select the emotions that come up when you think about this situation.

critic.title: What is your inner critic saying?
critic.description: Write down word for word what you tell yourself about this situation, one sentence per field.
critic.why: The critic is strongest when it speaks in the background. Written down, its words are easier to see — often harsher than anything you'd say to other people.
critic.placeholder: e.g. You always have to ruin everything.

response.title: Write your compassionate response

description.m: Write as if you were a caring friend who knows everything about you and loves you unconditionally. How would they answer the critic?
description.f: Write as if you were a caring friend who knows everything about you and loves you unconditionally. How would they answer the critic?

response.why: We usually have kind words ready for others, rarely for ourselves. Writing as a friend brings out that tone and eases the sense of threat that fuels self-criticism.

placeholder.m: Dear me, I want you to know that...
placeholder.f: Dear me, I want you to know that...

response.llmHint: Use this as inspiration — the letter should be in your own words:

takeaways.title: What resonated with you?
takeaways.description: Write one to three sentences from the letter that you want to remember, one per field.
takeaways.why: A short sentence is easier to recall than a whole letter the next time the critic speaks up.

intro.title: Positive Data Log
intro.description: The Positive Data Log helps you systematically collect evidence that contradicts a negative belief. Over time, this shifts the belief from "always true" to "sometimes true."
intro.step1: Create a target belief you want to challenge
intro.step2: Log evidence daily that contradicts it
intro.step3: Watch the belief weaken over time

targetBelief.title: What negative belief do you want to challenge?
targetBelief.description: Enter a general belief about yourself, others, or the world, such as “People can’t be trusted”. You can take one from the Core Beliefs exercise.
targetBelief.why: A negative belief mostly picks up what confirms it. The log deliberately collects what contradicts it — over time “always true” becomes “sometimes true”.
targetBelief.placeholder: e.g. “I always fail at important things”
targetBelief.believabilityTitle: How much do you believe this right now?

confirmation.description: Once created, you can return to this log daily to add evidence that contradicts the belief. Over time, you'll see the belief weaken.

log.addEvidenceDescription: Write down one event that doesn't fit this belief. Small ones count too.
log.addEvidenceWhy: Small events are easy to dismiss if you don't write them down. Collected together, they form a picture the belief can no longer ignore.
log.evidencePlaceholder: e.g. A colleague offered to help me with the project unprompted.
log.notesPlaceholder: What this event says about the belief...
log.rerateDescription: Considering the evidence you've collected, how much do you believe it now?
log.noEvidenceYet: No evidence logged yet. Start by adding your first entry above.

intro.title: Behavioral Experiment
intro.description: A behavioral experiment tests whether a belief you hold is actually true. Instead of arguing with the thought, you design a real-world test and observe what happens.
intro.howItWorksDescription: By comparing your prediction with what actually happens, you build a more accurate picture of reality and reduce the grip of unhelpful beliefs.

belief.title: What belief do you want to test?
belief.description: Write one belief you could check by doing something, ideally as “if…, then…”.
belief.why: You'll rate this belief again at the end. The gap between the two ratings shows how much the experience itself changed.
belief.placeholder: e.g., 'If I speak up in the meeting, everyone will think I'm stupid.'
belief.believabilityLabel: How strongly do you believe this right now? {value}%

prediction.title: What exactly do you expect to happen?
prediction.description: Describe an outcome you could later see or hear: what others will do, or what will happen to you.
prediction.why: A specific prediction can be checked against the facts afterwards. A vague “it'll go badly” can always be confirmed, even when nothing bad happened.
prediction.placeholder: e.g., 'People will roll their eyes or interrupt me within 10 seconds.'

confidenceLabel.m: How confident are you in this prediction? {value}%
confidenceLabel.f: How confident are you in this prediction? {value}%

design.title: Design your experiment
design.description: Describe one small, safe action that will test the prediction: what you'll do, where, and when.
design.why: Beliefs shift more through your own experience than through argument. A small test gives you real data without much risk.
design.placeholder: e.g., 'At tomorrow's team standup, I'll share one idea about the current project.'
design.whenLabel: When will you run this experiment? (optional)

safety.title: How might you play it safe during the test?
safety.description: List small ways you might hedge without thinking, e.g. speaking up only when the boss is away. These are called safety behaviors.
safety.why: Safety behaviors spoil the test: if nothing bad happens, you'll credit the hedge instead of learning the fear was overblown. Try to drop them.
safety.placeholder: e.g., 'Only speaking when I'm 100% sure of the answer'
safety.saveChoiceDescription: You can save this experiment as planned and come back later to record the outcome, or record the outcome right now.

outcome.title: What actually happened?
outcome.description: Stick to the facts: what happened and how others responded, the way a camera would record it.
outcome.learnedDescription: Compare the outcome with your prediction and note what it says about your belief.
outcome.learnedWhy: A clearly named conclusion is what makes the change stick. Without it, it's easy to write the result off as luck and slip back into the old belief.

learnedPlaceholder.m: The key thing I learned is...
learnedPlaceholder.f: The key thing I learned is...

outcome.rerateLabel: How strongly do you believe this now? {value}%

intro.title: Behavioral Activation
intro.description: When mood is low, we tend to withdraw from activities that once brought us joy or a sense of achievement. Behavioral Activation reverses this cycle by scheduling pleasant and meaningful activities, then tracking how they affect your mood.
intro.step1: Rate your current mood as a baseline
intro.step2: Plan at least 3 activities across different categories
intro.step3: Track your mood before and after each activity

moodBaseline.title: How are you feeling right now?
moodBaseline.description: Rate your overall mood on a scale of 0 to 10.
moodBaseline.why: This is your baseline. At the end of the week you'll compare it with your mood after activities and see what actually helps.
moodBaseline.weekStartDescription: Which week are you planning activities for?

planActivities.title: Plan your activities
planActivities.description: Add at least 3 small, specific activities, each with a day. Ideally from different categories.
planActivities.why: When mood is low, motivation tends to follow action, not come before it. Small scheduled steps break the cycle of withdrawal, and different categories lift mood in different ways.
planActivities.activityNamePlaceholder: e.g., Walk in the park, Call a friend...

summary.title: Your Week Plan
summary.trackDescription: Optionally mark activities as completed and rate your mood before and after each one. You can also save the plan now and track later.
summary.notesPlaceholder: Any reflections or observations about this week...

intro.title: Structured Problem Solving
intro.description: When problems feel overwhelming, breaking them into steps makes them manageable. This exercise uses a systematic approach from problem-solving therapy (D'Zurilla & Nezu) to help you define, brainstorm, evaluate, and act.
intro.howItWorksDescription: You'll generate multiple solutions without judgment, then evaluate each one to find the best path forward.

problem.title: What's the problem?
problem.description: Describe one specific situation: how things are now and what you want to be different.
problem.why: A vague “everything is falling apart” is paralysing. Naming how things are and how you want them to be shows what actually needs solving and makes ideas easier to find.
problem.placeholder: e.g., 'I've been putting off asking my boss for a raise for a month, and I want to have that talk before the quarter ends.'
problem.emotionsTitle: How are you feeling about this?
problem.emotionsDescription: Select the emotions this problem brings up for you.

brainstorm.title: What could you do about it?
brainstorm.description: Add at least 2 ideas, including unrealistic or odd ones. Don't judge them yet.
brainstorm.why: Judging while you generate shuts ideas down. Collecting many options first makes a good one more likely — often a blend of several others.
brainstorm.solutionPlaceholder: e.g., 'Book 15 minutes with my boss on Thursday'

evaluate.title: Evaluate your solutions
evaluate.description: For each idea, list pros and cons, then rate from 1 to 5 how doable it is and how well it would solve the problem.
evaluate.why: Applying the same criteria to every idea lets you compare them calmly instead of choosing out of anxiety or first impulse.
evaluate.effectivenessDescription: How well would it solve the problem?

choose.title: Choose your best solution
choose.description: Solutions are ranked by their average of feasibility and effectiveness. Select the one you want to commit to.
choose.actionPlanDescription: Briefly describe how you'll do it, then break it into first small steps below.
choose.actionPlanWhy: A decision without a plan tends to stay in your head. Small steps with a date turn it into action and show where to start.

review.title: Review Your Plan

markCompletedDescription.m: If you've already resolved this problem, you can record the outcome now. Otherwise, leave it as in-progress and come back later.
markCompletedDescription.f: If you've already resolved this problem, you can record the outcome now. Otherwise, leave it as in-progress and come back later.

review.outcomePlaceholder: What happened when you put the plan into action?
review.emotionsAfterDescription: Re-check your emotions after working through this problem.

intro.title: Graded Exposure Hierarchy
intro.description: Like climbing a ladder — you start with the easiest step and work your way up. By gradually facing feared situations, your anxiety naturally decreases over time.
intro.ladderDescription: You'll build a list of situations rated by how much distress they cause (0–100), then work through them from easiest to hardest.

fearTarget.fearDescription: Describe the fear, phobia, or anxiety you want to work on.
fearTarget.fearPlaceholder: e.g., Public speaking, spiders, social situations...

goalDescription.m: What would you like to be able to do when you've worked through this fear?
goalDescription.f: What would you like to be able to do when you've worked through this fear?

fearTarget.goalWhy: The goal at the top of the ladder reminds you why you're facing the fear. It helps you keep going when the steps get hard.
fearTarget.goalPlaceholder: e.g., Give a presentation at work confidently

buildHierarchy.title: Build your fear ladder
buildHierarchy.description: Add at least 3 specific situations linked to your fear. Rate how much anxiety each would cause: 0 is calm, 100 is the worst you can imagine.
buildHierarchy.why: A ladder lets you start with what you can already handle. Each rung you master shows you can cope and prepares you for the next.
buildHierarchy.situationPlaceholder: e.g., 'Ask one question in a team meeting'
buildHierarchy.tipDescription: Aim for 8–15 items spanning the full range (0–100). Include some easy ones (20–30) to build confidence.

safetyBehaviors.title: What do you do to feel safer when anxious?
safetyBehaviors.description: These are called safety behaviors: small ways of getting through a hard situation. List yours — common examples are below.
safetyBehaviors.why: They bring short-term relief but take away a key lesson: that you can cope without them. Once you know them, you can drop them step by step in later attempts.
safetyBehaviors.placeholder: e.g., Avoiding eye contact, checking phone...

log.lead: After each attempt, rate your anxiety from 0 to 100: before, at its worst, and after. Once it drops to half of where it started on a rung, you can move up.
log.why: The numbers show what anxiety hides: that each attempt gets a little easier and that you cope.
log.safetyUsed: Safety behaviours used in this attempt
log.notesPlaceholder: What do you notice after this attempt?

intro.title: Three Pathways to Meaning
intro.description: Viktor Frankl identified three ways we discover meaning in life. This exercise helps you explore each pathway and find your unique meaning balance.
intro.creativeDescription: What you give to the world through work, creation, and deeds.
intro.experientialDescription: What you receive from the world through love, beauty, and truth.
intro.attitudinalDescription: The stance you choose toward unavoidable suffering.
intro.quote: Life can be made meaningful in a threefold way: first, through what we give to life (creative values); second, by what we take from the world (experiential values); third, through the stand we take toward a fate we no longer can change (attitudinal values).
intro.emotionLabel: How are you feeling right now?

creative.title: What do you give to the world?
creative.description: List at least three things you do or create — at work, at home, for others. Use the slider to mark how much you put into each right now.
creative.why: Frankl held that meaning is found in concrete life, not in theory. The first pathway is what you create and give — listing it shows where meaning is already present and where it is thin.
creative.placeholder: e.g., Teaching others what I know, building software that helps people...
creative.engagementLabel: How much do you put into this now?

experiential.title: What do you receive from the world?
experiential.description: List at least three things you experience that matter to you: people, nature, music, moments of beauty. Use the slider to mark how much of it is in your life right now.
experiential.why: Frankl's second pathway: meaning also comes from what you receive — love, beauty, a real encounter with another person. You don't have to achieve anything for this pathway to be open.
experiential.placeholder: e.g., The feeling of connection with my partner, sunsets, listening to live music...
experiential.engagementLabel: How much of this is in your life now?

attitudinal.title: How do you face what can't be changed?
attitudinal.description: Think of a hardship you can't change: an illness, a loss, a limitation. Write the stance you take toward it, or want to take. One is enough.
attitudinal.why: Frankl's third pathway: when circumstances can't be changed, you still choose how you stand toward them. That freedom remains even when the other two pathways are closed.
attitudinal.placeholder: e.g., Choosing gratitude despite chronic illness, finding purpose in caregiving...
attitudinal.engagementLabel: How well are you able to hold this stance?

synthesis.title: Meaning Balance
synthesis.summaryText: You have {creative} creative, {experiential} experiential, and {attitudinal} attitudinal values.

intro.title: Socratic Self-Dialogue
intro.description: The answers are already within you. This exercise uses the Socratic method to help you discover them — a guided conversation that gently questions assumptions and illuminates what matters most.
intro.quote: What is to give light must endure burning.
intro.emotionLabel: How are you feeling right now?

focus.title: What would you like to explore?

description.m: I feel stuck or empty
description.f: I feel stuck or empty

values.label: Values
values.description: I want to understand my values

decision.label: Decision
decision.description: I need to make a difficult decision

focus.customPlaceholder: Describe what you'd like to explore...

context.title: Add Context
context.description: If you like, pick a journal entry or life area the topic relates to, or add something of your own. You can also skip this step.
context.additionalPlaceholder: Anything else you'd like the guide to know...

dialogue.title: Dialogue
dialogue.description: The guide asks questions rather than giving advice. Answer in your own words, as honestly as you can.
dialogue.why: In Socratic dialogue you reach the answers yourself. A conclusion put into your own words is more truly yours and stays with you longer than advice from outside.
dialogue.maxReached: Maximum exchanges reached. Let's capture your insights.
dialogue.continueOrFinish: You can continue or finish the conversation.

insights.title: Insights
insights.insightLabel: What is the most important insight from this conversation?
insights.rememberLabel: Which line from this conversation do you want to remember?
insights.rememberPlaceholder: e.g., a line worth coming back to...
insights.journalCheckbox: Create a journal entry from these insights

intro.title: Mountain Range of Meaning
intro.description: Your life is a landscape of peaks and valleys. Each peak represents a moment of deep meaning; each valley, a time of struggle that shaped you. Together, they form your unique mountain range.

peaksDescription.m: Moments when you felt most alive, fulfilled, or certain life had meaning.
peaksDescription.f: Moments when you felt most alive, fulfilled, or certain life had meaning.

intro.valleysDescription: Moments of deepest struggle, loss, or difficulty — and what they taught you.
intro.emotionLabel: How are you feeling right now?

peaks.title: When did life feel most meaningful?
peaks.description: Describe 3–7 moments when life felt fullest and most meaningful. For each, add your age and what gave it meaning.
peaks.why: Peaks show what has already carried meaning in your life. The same sources — people, work, values — can often be found again.

valleys.title: When was life hardest?
valleys.description: Describe 2–5 of your hardest times: struggle, loss, crisis. For each, add your age and what it taught you.
valleys.why: Frankl showed that suffering too can hold meaning — through how we respond to it. The point isn't that "it was worth it", but what it left in you.
valleys.takeYourTime: Take your time with this. There's no rush.

timeline.title: Your Mountain Range
timeline.description: Here is the landscape of your life. Click any point to see details.

themes.title: Discover Your Themes
themes.why: Single memories are anecdotes; recurring threads show what truly gives you meaning. The final step builds on them.
themes.peaksCommonLabel: What do your peaks have in common?
themes.valleysCommonLabel: What do your valleys have in common?
themes.connectionLabel: Did any valley lead to a later peak that wouldn't have happened without it?
themes.connectionPlaceholder: e.g., losing that job pushed me to...

future.title: What could your next peak be?
future.description: Write 1–3 things you want to do or experience in the coming years, drawing on what your peaks had in common.
future.why: Frankl said meaning also waits ahead of us — in what life still asks of us. Plans grounded in your own peaks have a real source.
future.peakPlaceholder: e.g., plan a family trip, finish my own project...

intro.title: Paradoxical Intention Lab
intro.description: Viktor Frankl's paradoxical intention technique breaks anticipatory anxiety by deliberately wishing for the very thing you fear — with humor. By exaggerating the fear to absurdity, you create psychological distance from it.
intro.example1: A man who feared sweating was told to show everyone how much he could sweat: "I only sweated out a quart before, but now I'm going to sweat at least ten quarts!"
intro.example2: A bookkeeper who feared making errors was told to intentionally make as many errors as possible. His anxiety disappeared, and so did his errors.
intro.keyInsight: Key insight: Humor creates distance. When you laugh at a fear, it loses its grip.
intro.boundaryText: This exercise is designed for everyday anxieties and anticipatory fears. It is not suitable for deep trauma, severe phobias, or situations involving real danger. If your fears are related to trauma, please work with a professional.
intro.emotionLabel: How are you feeling right now?

fears.title: Which fears feed on themselves?
fears.description: Write 1–3 everyday fears that grow the harder you try to control them — e.g., blushing, stuttering, sleeplessness.
fears.why: Paradoxical intention targets anticipatory anxiety — fear that brings on the very thing it dreads (worrying about insomnia makes it harder to fall asleep). So you start by naming such a loop.
fears.whatPlaceholder: e.g., Making a fool of myself in front of others...
fears.whatHappensLabel: What exactly do you expect will happen?
fears.whatHappensPlaceholder: e.g., I'll start stuttering and everyone will stare...

craft.title: Wish for what you fear
craft.description: Write one sentence in which you wish for exactly what you fear — exaggerated to the point of absurdity. The funnier, the better.
craft.why: A fear you try to suppress grows. When you exaggerate it with humor, you gain distance and the tension drops. Humor doesn't dismiss the problem; it takes away the fear's gravity.
craft.placeholder: e.g., I'll tremble so violently I register on the Richter scale!

practice.title: What will you tell yourself when the fear shows up?
practice.description: For each fear, write a short line you will say to yourself the moment you feel the first tension.
practice.why: A line prepared in advance is easier to recall under stress than one invented on the spot. The paradox only works in a real situation, not on paper.
practice.scriptPlaceholder: When I feel [the fear], I'll tell myself: "Great, now I get to [your intention]…"

intro.title: Dereflection Practice
intro.description: When we fixate on a problem, it grows larger. Dereflection is Viktor Frankl's technique for redirecting attention away from the self and toward something meaningful in the world.
intro.quote: Being human always points, and is directed, to something, or someone, other than oneself.
intro.emotionLabel: How are you feeling right now?

fixation.title: Where is your attention stuck?
fixation.why: Dereflection starts by naming what your attention keeps circling. The more it consumes, the more your attention needs somewhere else to go — the next step is about that.
fixation.whatLabel: What problem, symptom, or concern keeps consuming your attention?
fixation.whatPlaceholder: Describe what you keep thinking about...
fixation.energyLabel: How much mental energy does this consume daily?
fixation.impactLabel: How is this affecting your daily life?
fixation.impactPlaceholder: Describe the impact on your daily activities, relationships, mood...

redirections.title: Where could your attention go instead?
redirections.description: List at least three specific activities, people, or causes outside yourself that matter to you and that you want to give your attention to.
redirections.why: Frankl noticed that fighting an intrusive thought only strengthens it. Attention frees up when it has something meaningful to rest on — so you look for a focus outside yourself, not a way to "stop thinking".
redirections.suggestionsSubtext: These life areas are going well and could nourish you:
redirections.activityPlaceholder: e.g., Volunteering at the community garden, calling my sister...

commit.title: What will you do this week?
commit.description: Tick 1–2 activities. For each, write when you will do it and how you will return to it when your thoughts drift off again.
commit.why: A specific time turns a good intention into a plan. A way back prepared in advance means a returning thought isn't a failure, just a cue to come back.
commit.whenPlaceholder: e.g., Tuesday and Thursday evenings after dinner
commit.pullbackLabel: What will you do when your thoughts drift back to the problem?
commit.pullbackPlaceholder: e.g., I'll notice the thought, take a breath, and redirect to...

intro.title: Tragic Optimism
intro.description: Life includes suffering, guilt, and the awareness that our time is limited. Tragic optimism is the ability to say "yes" to life in spite of everything — to find meaning not despite these realities, but through engaging with them honestly.
intro.quote: In some way, suffering ceases to be suffering at the moment it finds a meaning, such as the meaning of a sacrifice.
intro.warningText: This exercise explores deep personal themes. If you're working through significant trauma, grief, or existential distress, consider doing this with a therapist or counselor who can provide professional support.
intro.emotionLabel: How are you feeling right now?

focus.title: Which of the three hardships do you want to work with today?
focus.why: Frankl called suffering, guilt, and finitude the "tragic triad" — three things no one escapes. Each calls for different questions, so you choose one.

description.m: Something I'm going through or have been through
description.f: Something I'm going through or have been through

description.m: Something I feel responsible for or regret
description.f: Something I feel responsible for or regret

finitude.label: Finitude
finitude.description: My awareness of limited time and what it means for how I live

write.title: Write Freely
write.description: Write freely about your experience of the theme you chose. A few sentences are enough — don't edit or judge.
write.why: Writing freely about a hard experience sorts out your thoughts and eases tension. It also gives a starting point for the next questions and the conversation.

guided.title: Guided Reflection
guided.why: The questions lead from describing the hardship to what it says about your values and what you can do with it. That, for Frankl, is where meaning can be found.

suffering.q1: What is the suffering you're carrying? Describe it as honestly as you can.
suffering.q2: Has this suffering changed you, and how?
suffering.q3: If this suffering could speak, what would it say it's trying to teach you?

q1.m: What do you feel guilty about? Describe it specifically and honestly.
q1.f: What do you feel guilty about? Describe it specifically and honestly.

guilt.q2: What matters to you so much that breaking it hurts this much?

q3.m: If you could partially make amends or learn from this, what would that look like?
q3.f: If you could partially make amends or learn from this, what would that look like?

finitude.q1: When you think about the fact that your time is limited, what feelings arise?
finitude.q2: How does awareness of finitude change what matters to you?

q3.m: If you fully accepted that your time is limited, what would you do differently starting today?
q3.f: If you fully accepted that your time is limited, what would you do differently starting today?

dialogue.title: Dialogue
dialogue.description: The guide will ask a few questions about your notes from the previous steps. Answer in your own words; you can end the conversation at any time.
dialogue.reminder: Remember, working with a professional can deepen this exploration.
dialogue.completed: You've completed the dialogue. Let's capture your insights.

insights.title: Insights
insights.meaningLabel: What meaning, if any, have you found?
insights.carryLabel: What will you carry forward from this reflection?

intro.title: Attitudinal Shift
intro.quote: Everything can be taken from a man but one thing: the last of the human freedoms — to choose one's attitude in any given set of circumstances, to choose one's own way.
intro.description: This exercise helps you transform the stories you tell yourself about unavoidable circumstances. You'll identify "because" statements — the narratives that keep you stuck — and find your choice point.

exampleBefore.m: Because I lost my job, I'm a failure.
exampleBefore.f: Because I lost my job, I'm a failure.

exampleAfter.m: Although I lost my job, I choose to see this as an opportunity to find work that aligns with my values.
exampleAfter.f: Although I lost my job, I choose to see this as an opportunity to find work that aligns with my values.

intro.exampleNote: The circumstances don't change. Your relationship to them does.
intro.emotionLabel: How are you feeling right now?

statements.title: Which "because…" sentences hold you back?
statements.description: Write at least three sentences where a circumstance you can't change decides things for you: "Because…, I can't…" or "Because…, I am…".
statements.why: A "because" sentence ties a fact to a conclusion as if the conclusion were inevitable. Once it's written down, you can see the fact is fixed but the conclusion isn't.
statements.shadowTitle: Your shadow beliefs — click one to start a sentence from it:

placeholder.m: e.g., "Because I grew up poor, I'll never feel financially secure..."
placeholder.f: e.g., "Because I grew up poor, I'll never feel financially secure..."

shift.title: Where do you have a choice here?
shift.helpButton: Help me see where I have a choice
shift.formatHint: Keep the fact, change the conclusion: "Although [what happened], I choose to [how you want to respond]".
shift.why: Frankl called this the last of the human freedoms: circumstances may be beyond your control, but your stance toward them is not. The "Although…, I choose…" sentence practices that freedom.

review.title: Your Shifts
review.surprisedLabel: Which reframe surprised you the most?
review.trueSelfLabel: Which one feels most true to who you want to be?

summary.title: Summary
summary.commitmentCheckbox: Create a commitment to practice a reframe this week

intro.title: Legacy Letter
intro.description: Viktor Frankl believed that awareness of our finite time can be our greatest motivator. This exercise invites you to write a letter from the perspective of having lived a full, meaningful life.
intro.secondaryDescription: What would you want to say? What would you want others to know? This isn't about perfection — it's about connecting with what truly matters to you.

quote.m: Live as if you were living already for the second time and as if you had acted the first time as wrongly as you are about to act now.
quote.f: Live as if you were living already for the second time and as if you had acted the first time as wrongly as you are about to act now.

intro.emotionLabel: How are you feeling right now?

warmup.title: Before you write
warmup.description: Click 2–3 questions that speak to you and answer them briefly. They'll serve as material for your letter.

prompts.p1: What do you want your children, family, or community to know about what mattered to you?
prompts.p2: What impact do you want to have had on the world?

p3.m: What wisdom have you earned through experience that you want to pass on?
p3.f: What wisdom have you earned through experience that you want to pass on?

prompts.p4: What would make you feel your time was well-spent?

p5.m: What do you want to be remembered for?
p5.f: What do you want to be remembered for?

write.title: Your Letter
write.description: Write a letter as yourself near the end of a long, well-lived life — to your loved ones, to the world, or to yourself today. A few paragraphs are enough.
write.why: Looking back from the end of life separates what truly matters from day-to-day concerns. Frankl held that awareness of finitude doesn't take meaning away; it urges us to act on it.

hint.m: Consider including: what you've created and contributed, the relationships that shaped you, the suffering you overcame and what it taught you, the values you lived by.
hint.f: Consider including: what you've created and contributed, the relationships that shaped you, the suffering you overcame and what it taught you, the values you lived by.

reflect.title: Reflect
reflect.description: Would you like to discuss your letter, or move on?

truthLabel.m: What felt most true in what you wrote?
truthLabel.f: What felt most true in what you wrote?

safetyBanner.checkboxLabel: I understand this is self-exploration, not therapy

intro.title: Parts Mapping
intro.description: In IFS, we all have different "parts" — inner voices, feelings, or impulses that each have a role in our life. This exercise helps you map them out.

managers.title: Managers
managers.description: Strategic parts that try to keep you safe by controlling your life (e.g., The Perfectionist, The Planner)

firefighters.title: Firefighters
firefighters.description: Reactive parts that extinguish pain when it breaks through (e.g., The Comfort Eater, The Netflix Binger)

exiles.title: Exiles
exiles.description: Vulnerable parts that carry old pain, often hidden by protectors (e.g., Little Me, The Lonely Child)

intro.quote: Every part has a positive intention, even the ones that cause us trouble.
intro.emotionLabel: How are you feeling right now? (optional)

trailhead.title: Start with a Trailhead
trailhead.description: Recall a recent moment when your reaction was stronger than the situation called for — that’s your trailhead. Describe it below.
trailhead.why: A reaction that feels too big for the situation is a sign that a part has stepped in. Starting from a real moment lets you find parts where they actually operate, not in theory.

bodyLocationLabel.m: Where did you feel it in your body?
bodyLocationLabel.f: Where did you feel it in your body?

trailhead.thoughtsLabel: What thoughts or inner voice showed up?
trailhead.thoughtsPlaceholder: e.g., “You’ll mess this up again”, “Something bad is going to happen”

identifyPart.title: Name This Part
identifyPart.description: Give a name to a part that speaks up in you — for example, the one from the moment you described. Then answer the questions as far as you can.
identifyPart.why: A named part becomes someone you can get to know, not the whole of you. The questions below help you see what role it plays and what drives it.

nameLabel.m: What would you call this part?
nameLabel.f: What would you call this part?

identifyPart.namePlaceholder: e.g., The Worrier, The Controller, Little Me
identifyPart.protectionLabel: What is it trying to protect you from?
identifyPart.protectionPlaceholder: e.g., Being rejected, failing, feeling helpless
identifyPart.fearLabel: What is it afraid would happen if it stopped?

fearPlaceholder.m: e.g., Everything would fall apart, I'd be overwhelmed
fearPlaceholder.f: e.g., Everything would fall apart, I'd be overwhelmed

identifyPart.bodyLabel: Where do you feel this part in your body? (optional)
identifyPart.roleHint: You don’t have to know yet — the role can be changed later.
identifyPart.exileCarriesLabel: What does this part carry? What pain or belief?
identifyPart.exileCarriesPlaceholder: e.g., feeling like a burden; childhood shame; “nobody wants me”
identifyPart.exileNeedsLabel: What does it need from you?
identifyPart.exileNeedsPlaceholder: e.g., to be noticed; safety; not to be alone

visualMap.title: Your Parts Map
visualMap.why: Parts rarely act alone: some protect others, some pull in opposite directions. The connections on the map show where inner conflicts come from.

instructions.tapTwo: Click two parts to draw a connection

reflection.description: Look at your map and write down what surprises you or what keeps repeating.
reflection.why: Looking at your parts from the outside, you see them instead of being them — that’s already a bit of unblending. From there, patterns are easier to spot.
reflection.aiButton: Get AI Insights on Your Map

aiDisclaimer.m: This reflection is based on patterns in what you've shared. Your inner system is uniquely yours.
aiDisclaimer.f: This reflection is based on patterns in what you've shared. Your inner system is uniquely yours.

lifeAreas.title: Life Area Connections
lifeAreas.description: For each part, select the life areas it affects most.
lifeAreas.emptyState: No life areas defined yet. You can add them later in the Life Areas section.

checkIn.title: Unblending Practice
checkIn.subtitle: Creating space between you and your parts — 2-3 minutes
checkIn.description: When we're "blended" with a part, we are the anxiety, the anger, the perfectionism. Unblending means stepping back into the calm observer seat — your Self.
checkIn.emotionLabel: How are you feeling right now?

awareness.title: Notice What's Here
awareness.description: Is a strong feeling or reaction running the show right now — so that it feels like you, rather than something you’re experiencing?
awareness.why: As long as a feeling seems to be you, you can’t step back from it. Noticing and naming it is the first step of unblending — often it already makes a little room.

options.yes: Yes — something is really active right now

awareness.noResponse: That's great. Let's practice noticing anyway — it's a useful skill for when parts do activate.
awareness.partLabel: Does this feel like a part you know? (optional)

magicQuestion.title: The Magic Question
magicQuestion.question: How do you FEEL TOWARD this feeling or part?

description.m: If you feel curious, compassionate, or calm toward it — that's your Self. If you feel annoyed, scared, or critical — that's another part reacting to the first one.
description.f: If you feel curious, compassionate, or calm toward it — that's your Self. If you feel annoyed, scared, or critical — that's another part reacting to the first one.

magicQuestion.why: In IFS, a part shifts only when it senses the Self looking at it. When one part fights another, both usually grow stronger.

selfEnergy.m: I feel curious, open, or compassionate
selfEnergy.f: I feel curious, open, or compassionate

reactive.m: I feel frustrated, scared, or judgmental
reactive.f: I feel frustrated, scared, or judgmental

secondaryCheck.title: Another Part Arrived

description.m: That frustration, fear, or judgment is another part. Can you ask it to step back just a little, so you can get curious about the first part?
description.f: That frustration, fear, or judgment is another part. Can you ask it to step back just a little, so you can get curious about the first part?

secondaryCheck.why: A part reacting to another (say, anger at your own fear) blocks access to the first one. Asking it for a little room usually works better than arguing with it.
secondaryCheck.breathingPrompt: Click to begin the breathing exercise
secondaryCheck.afterQuestion: How do you feel toward the original part now?

better.m: I feel more curious or compassionate now
better.f: I feel more curious or compassionate now

partLabel.m: What would you call this second part? (optional)
partLabel.f: What would you call this second part? (optional)

secondaryCheck.stillReactiveTitle: This second part needs attention now
secondaryCheck.stillReactiveHint: In IFS, when the second part won’t step back, it becomes the target — we don’t push past it to the first one. You can also simply finish for today.
secondaryCheck.switchTargetButton: I’ll turn to this second part

steppingBack.title: Ask the Part to Step Back
steppingBack.description: Now, gently ask the part if it would be willing to step back just a little. Not go away — just give you some breathing room.
steppingBack.why: Parts rarely disappear on command, but they often agree to make some room when asked kindly. That space is where the Self shows up.
steppingBack.shiftLabel: What do you notice after asking?
steppingBack.shiftPlaceholder: e.g., my shoulders dropped a little; the fear is still there, but further away

closing.title: How Much Space Do You Feel?
closing.thankPart: Thank the part for making room for you — even a little. It took the risk.

partSelect.title: Talking with a Part of Yourself
partSelect.description: Have a conversation with one of your parts. The AI models what the part might say, based on what you know about it — treat the replies as prompts for your own inner listening, not as your part’s actual voice.
partSelect.emptyState: You need to create parts first. Go to Parts Mapping to identify and name your parts.

label.m: Which part would you like to speak with?

label.f: Which protector would you like to appreciate?

understandJob.why: A protector usually does something difficult for a good reason. Once you understand what it guards against and what it fears, thanking it comes easier than fighting it.
understandJob.triggersLabel: What does this protector protect you from?

safety.title: Exile Witnessing

description.m: This exercise guides you in gently approaching an exile — a vulnerable part that carries old pain or beliefs. You'll check in with protectors first, then simply be present with the exile and offer compassion.
description.f: This exercise guides you in gently approaching an exile — a vulnerable part that carries old pain or beliefs. You'll check in with protectors first, then simply be present with the exile and offer compassion.

safety.disclaimer: This is not unburdening — it's witnessing. You're creating a moment of connection, not trying to fix or heal. That deeper work is best done with a therapist.

protectorCheck.title: Getting Permission
protectorCheck.description: Select the protectors that might guard this exile. Then silently ask them for permission and choose what they answer.
protectorCheck.why: Protectors guard an exile because they fear its pain will flood you. Asking permission respects their role — going around them usually makes them come back stronger.
protectorCheck.silentQuestion: Close your eyes. Silently ask: "Is it okay if I approach this exile?"

yes.label: Yes, go ahead
yes.description: The protectors feel safe enough to step aside

hesitant.label: Hesitant but okay
hesitant.description: They're nervous but willing to trust you

no.label: Not yet
no.description: They're not ready — the exile is too vulnerable right now

protectorCheck.blockingMessage: That's okay — the protectors aren't ready. Try the Protector Appreciation exercise first to build trust with them.

approach.title: Approaching the Exile
approach.description: Go slowly. Turn your attention inward and sense the vulnerable part. Mark what you notice — whatever comes on its own is enough.
approach.why: Questions about body, age and emotion help you sense the part as someone specific, separate from you. That makes it easier to be with it, not in it.
approach.bodyLocationLabel: Where do you sense it in your body?
approach.feltAgeLabel: How old does this part feel?
approach.emotionLabel: What emotion is this part holding?

witness.title: Being Present
witness.description: Stay with this part and listen — you don’t need to fix anything. If something comes, write down what it wants you to know and what it came to believe.
witness.why: An exile has usually waited a long time to be seen. Simply listening, without fixing, is the heart of witnessing in IFS.

messagePlaceholder.m: What does this part want you to know?
messagePlaceholder.f: What does this part want you to know?

witness.beliefPlaceholder: What does it believe about you or the world?
witness.beliefNote: In IFS, these beliefs are called "burdens" — things the exile took on from painful experiences.

description.f: What would you like to say to this part?

compassion.why: An exile often still lives in that old moment, alone with the pain. Words from the Self show it that someone is with it now.

closing.distressedWarning: Being seen sometimes brings up more feeling — that's normal and not a sign something went wrong. If this persists, consider sharing with a therapist who can provide deeper support.

prerequisites.description: Parts form alliances, oppositions, and cascading chains. A Perfectionist and Procrastinator might look opposite but both protect the same wounded exile.

mapRelationships.title: How Do They Relate?
mapRelationships.description: For each pair, choose how they affect each other: polarized parts pull in opposite directions, allied ones support each other, “protects” means one guards the other.
mapRelationships.why: Inner conflicts rarely involve just one part. Seeing the pairs makes it easier to spot which parts clash and which work together.

polarizationDeepDive.title: Exploring Polarizations
polarizationDeepDive.description: Polarized parts are often the most revealing — they may both be protecting the same wound.
polarizationDeepDive.why: When each side hears what the other thinks, it usually becomes clear that both want good things for you. That softens the fight and reveals what they both protect.
