intro.title: A moment of gratitude
intro.description: Gratitude works best when you notice it on purpose. Think back over today — what was good, even if small?

title.m: What are you grateful for today?
title.f: What are you grateful for today?

items.description: Three things are enough. Being specific helps: instead of “family” — “coffee and a chat with mom”.
items.why: Noticing good things on purpose balances an attention that naturally picks up mostly on problems. Being specific takes you back to the moment, not just to a label.

why.title: Why does this one matter today?
why.description: Pick one thing from your list and write why it matters to you. (Optional.)
why.why: Thinking about why something matters deepens gratitude and links it to what you care about.

moment.title: The best moment of your day
moment.description: What was the most pleasant thing today? It can be tiny — a taste, a view, someone's gesture.

pleasantness.title: How pleasant was it?
pleasantness.description: Use the slider to mark how pleasant the moment was for you.
pleasantness.why: Pausing on a pleasant moment, even just to rate it, lets you live it once more.

senses.title: Go back there for a moment
senses.description: Bring the moment back and describe the details: what you see, hear and feel, any taste or smell.
senses.why: Sensory details bring back the experience itself, not just the memory of a fact. The more precisely you describe them, the more the pleasure returns.
senses.placeholder: I see… I hear… I feel…

intro.title: Self-compassion break
intro.description: Three steps: notice that this is hard, remember you're not the only one, and say something kind to yourself. You don't have to fix anything.

mindfulness.title: Mindfulness: what hurts right now?
mindfulness.description: Name what is hard right now in a sentence or two. Without judging yourself or the situation.
mindfulness.why: Putting a difficulty into words usually eases the tension a little. To take care of yourself, you first have to notice that you are struggling.

humanity.title: Common humanity: who else knows this?
humanity.description: Write who else might feel something similar in a situation like this. Struggling is part of being human.
humanity.why: Struggling suggests that something is wrong only with you. Remembering that others go through the same eases the sense of being alone.

kindness.title: Kind words to yourself
kindness.description: Write yourself one sentence, the kind someone who truly cares about you would say.
kindness.why: The tone you use with yourself shapes how you feel. Kind words soothe much like support from someone close.
kindness.placeholder: I want to tell myself that…

see.title: 5 things you can see
see.description: Look around slowly. Name five things within sight.
see.why: Naming what your senses pick up moves attention from anxious thoughts to what is happening here and now. That helps your body settle.

feel.title: 4 things you can feel
feel.description: For example the ground under your feet, clothes on your skin, the air temperature.

hear.title: 3 sounds you can hear
hear.description: Near and far. Listen for a moment.

smell.title: 2 things you can smell
smell.description: If there are none, name two you like.

taste.title: 1 thing you can taste
taste.description: The taste in your mouth right now — or one you like.

before.title: How do you feel right now?
before.description: Mark your emotions before the exercise — you'll compare them afterwards. You can skip this.

breath.title: Breathe in a box rhythm
breath.description: The bottom wall of the square is the phase you are in. Change the phase lengths next to the walls.
breath.why: A steady, slow breathing rhythm signals your body that it can slow down. Counting also occupies your attention, so thoughts circle less.

after.title: And how about now?
after.description: Mark your emotions after the exercise. You can skip this.

win.title: What went well today?
win.description: One thing is enough — even a small one. What matters is that it's yours.
win.why: Attention easily locks onto what went wrong. Noticing small wins strengthens the sense that you have a say in your day.

meaning.title: What does it say about you?
meaning.description: What strength or skill of yours made it happen? For example persistence, patience, courage.
meaning.why: Linking a win to a trait of yours builds a self-image based on evidence, not only on slip-ups.

before.title: How do you feel right now?
before.description: Mark your emotions before the exercise so you can compare them afterwards. You can skip this.

breath.title: Breathe with a longer exhale
breath.description: The bottom wall of the square is the phase you are in. Change the phase lengths next to the walls.
breath.why: A longer exhale calms the body. The breath is there to help you approach something hard, not to make the emotion disappear.

after.title: And how about now?
after.description: Mark your emotions after the exercise. You can skip this.

hadEpisode.title: Did anger show up today?
hadEpisode.why: Logging a calm day matters as much as logging a hard one: it shows what helps and gives a true picture of how often anger shows up.

quietDay.title: What helped you stay calm today?

intensity.title: How strong was the anger at its worst?
intensity.description: 0 is calm, 10 is anger that was hard to control.

trigger.title: What happened?
trigger.description: Describe it the way a camera would record it: who, what, where.
trigger.why: A camera-style account separates facts from interpretation. It becomes easier to see what happened and what a thought added.
trigger.placeholder: A colleague cut me off in a meeting…

title.m: How did you notice the anger building?
title.f: How did you notice the anger building?

firstSign.description: The first signal in your body or thoughts: a tight jaw, heat in your face, clenched hands. (Optional.)
firstSign.why: The early signal is the easiest point to stop. Over time you'll start recognising it before the anger grows.

thought.title: Which thought fuelled it?
thought.description: It often sounds like “he shouldn't do that”, “she's doing it on purpose” or “it's always like this”.
thought.why: Anger grows not only from the situation but from how you explain it to yourself. A thought written down can be checked later.

behavior.description: Your reaction, without judging it. Include what you managed to hold back.

placeholder.m: I raised my voice and left…
placeholder.f: I raised my voice and left…

helped.title: What helped, or what would help next time?
helped.description: A pause, a breath, a different thought, talking later. (Optional.)

intro.title: Your anger map
intro.description: Anger doesn't come out of nowhere. It has triggers, body signals and typical reactions. Gathering them in one place helps you notice anger earlier.

triggers.title: What angers you most often?
triggers.description: Situations, other people's behaviour, times of day, tiredness. Five is a lot, three is enough.

bodySigns.title: What are the first signals in your body?
bodySigns.description: What shows up before the anger erupts: heat, tension, faster breathing.
bodySigns.why: Your body usually reacts before you're aware of the anger. Knowing your signals lets you stop earlier.

reaction.title: How do you usually react?
reaction.description: Shouting, sarcasm, silence, slamming doors, blaming yourself. No judging.

cost.title: What does this reaction cost you?
cost.description: What do you lose because of it in relationships, at work and in how you feel afterwards?
cost.why: Naming the costs shows why the reaction is worth changing — for your own reasons, not because anger is “bad”.

protects.title: What does your anger protect you from?
protects.description: Anger often guards something important: boundaries or a sense of fairness. It can also shield you from helplessness or shame. (Optional.)
protects.why: Once you know what your anger guards, you can look after it directly, without the outburst.

intro.title: A plan for when anger rises

description.m: A pause is easier when you decide in advance when and how. An “if…, then…” plan works better than simply resolving to be calmer.
description.f: A pause is easier when you decide in advance when and how. An “if…, then…” plan works better than simply resolving to be calmer.

earlySigns.title: What are your three earliest signs of anger?
earlySigns.description: Signals in your body, thoughts or behaviour. You can take them from your anger log or map.
earlySigns.why: The earlier the signal, the easier it is to stop: the anger is still weak and you still have a choice in how to react.

ifThen.title: If I notice…, then…
ifThen.description: Write one sentence with a concrete action. For example: “If I feel heat in my face, I'll say I need five minutes and step into the hallway”.
ifThen.why: An “if…, then…” plan links a signal to a ready action. In the moment you don't have to come up with anything, just do what you already decided.

returnPromise.title: How will you return to the conversation?
returnPromise.description: A pause isn't running away. Decide what you'll say as you step out and when you'll come back.
returnPromise.why: The other person accepts a pause more easily when they know you'll come back. And coming back is easier when the words and the time are ready.
returnPromise.placeholder: I'll say: “Let's come back to this in fifteen minutes”…

confidence.title: How confident are you that this will work?
confidence.description: If it's under 50, simplify the plan or pick an earlier signal.

observation.title: What happened? Just the facts
observation.description: Describe it like a camera, without judgements or interpretations. Instead of “he ignored me again” write “he didn't answer three messages”.
observation.why: Facts without judgement are easier for the other person to hear and harder to argue with. Separating them from interpretation often eases the anger by itself.

feeling.title: What do you feel besides anger?
feeling.description: Underneath anger there's often something else: hurt, fear, tiredness, disappointment. Pick what fits.
feeling.why: Anger often covers feelings that are harder to show. Naming them makes it easier to see what you need.

needs.title: What was missing for you in this situation?
needs.description: Pick the need that went unmet. One or several.
needs.why: Anger usually defends a need. Once you name it, you can look after it directly instead of fighting the other person.

needNote.title: Anything else about this need?
needNote.description: If no name fits, describe the need in your own words. (Optional.)

request.title: What can you ask for?
request.description: A concrete, doable request the other person can answer with “yes” or “no”. For example: “Could you let me know if you're running late?”.
request.why: A concrete request can be met. A general expectation like “respect me” is easy to misread or dismiss.

hadMoment.title: Was there a moment of shame recently?
hadMoment.description: Embarrassment counts too, as does feeling that something is wrong with you or wanting to hide.

description.m: A moment when you didn't have to hide anything. (Optional.)
description.f: A moment when you didn't have to hide anything. (Optional.)

situation.title: What happened?
situation.description: Briefly: the situation and who was there, if anyone.

body.title: What was happening in your body?
body.description: Shame often shows in the body: a hot face, lowered eyes, wanting to disappear. (Optional.)

compass.description: These are four typical reactions to shame. Pick the closest one.
compass.why: Shame usually sets off one of four automatic reactions. Recognising yours makes it easier to catch it next time.

criticSaid.title: What did the inner critic say?
criticSaid.description: Write its words down literally, even if they're harsh.
criticSaid.why: Written down, the critic's words can be seen from a distance. It's easier to notice how harsh they are and answer them in the next step.

kindVoice.title: What would a kind person say?
kindVoice.description: Someone who knows you well and wishes you well. They don't have to deny the facts, only stop judging.
kindVoice.why: Shame eases with kindness, not punishment. The more you practise a gentle voice, the more easily it shows up on its own.

intro.title: Your shame map
intro.description: Shame likes to hide, and once named it loses some of its power. This map shows where it speaks up, how you react to it and which demand on yourself sits behind it.

areas.title: Where does shame speak up most often?

bodySigns.title: What are the body signals of shame?
bodySigns.description: For example a hot face, lowered eyes, hunched shoulders. Write one to three.
bodySigns.why: The body usually gives shame away sooner than thoughts do. Knowing your signals, you'll notice earlier that shame is speaking up.

compass.title: How do you usually react to shame?
compass.description: The compass of shame (Nathanson) describes four reactions. Pick the ones you recognise in yourself.
compass.why: Knowing your usual reactions makes it easier to catch them as they happen and look after yourself instead.

audience.title: Who are you ashamed in front of?
audience.description: Shame can be about what others will think, or about what you think of yourself.

standard.title: What demand on yourself sits behind your shame?

description.m: Write it as one sentence starting with “I should…”. For example: “I should always cope”, “I should know everything at work”.
description.f: Write it as one sentence starting with “I should…”. For example: “I should always cope”, “I should know everything at work”.

why.m: Once the demand has a name, you can check it: is it realistic, and would you hold someone close to you to it? Shame often guards rules no one can meet.
why.f: Once the demand has a name, you can check it: is it realistic, and would you hold someone close to you to it? Shame often guards rules no one can meet.

origin.title: Where did this demand come from?
origin.description: Who did it come from, or what experience taught it? For example home, school, work. (Optional.)
origin.why: Seeing where a demand came from makes it easier to treat it as a rule you took on, not a truth about you. Then you can decide whether to keep it.

facts.title: What happened? Just the facts
facts.description: Describe the situation without judging yourself.

statement.title: Finish the sentence: I feel bad because…
statement.description: Write whatever comes to mind first.

verdict.title: What is that sentence about?

description.m: Guilt says “I did something bad”, shame says “I am bad”. The difference points to what can help.
description.f: Guilt says “I did something bad”, shame says “I am bad”. The difference points to what can help.

verdict.why: Guilt is eased by repair, shame by kindness towards yourself. That is why the next step depends on this answer.

repair.title: How can you make it right?
repair.description: Write one concrete step: an apology, a fix, an explanation or a conversation.
repair.why: Repair settles guilt better than dwelling on it: the bad feeling turns into an action that changes something.

kindVoice.title: What would a kind person say?
kindVoice.description: What would someone who knows you and is on your side say? Write their words down.
kindVoice.why: Punishing yourself doesn't ease shame. It softens when you meet kindness, including your own.

intro.title: Your compassionate image
intro.description: Compassion-focused therapy builds an image of an ideally kind figure. It can be a person, an animal, a light or a place. It doesn't have to resemble anyone real. What matters is how you feel with it.

wisdom.title: Wisdom: what does this figure understand?
wisdom.description: It understands that life can be hard and no one chose their brain or their history. Describe how that wisdom shows.
wisdom.why: The compassionate image has four qualities: wisdom, strength, warmth and no judgement. The more clearly you picture it, the easier it is to call up in a hard moment.

strength.title: Strength: how does it show its calm?
strength.description: It is calm and steady, your difficult emotions don't overwhelm it. Describe how that shows.

warmth.title: Warmth: how does it sound and look?
warmth.description: It wishes you well. Describe its voice, its face and the way it looks at you.

nonJudgement.title: No judgement: how do you feel with it?
nonJudgement.description: It doesn't criticise or condemn you. Describe how you feel in its presence.

message.title: What does it say to you?
message.description: Imagine it looking at you in a hard moment. What sentence do you hear from it?
message.why: You can call up this sentence when the inner critic speaks up.

intro.title: Worry time
intro.description: When a worry shows up during the day, note it in one sentence and set it aside until now. This is the time to come back to them. Pick a fixed time, ideally early evening, not right before bed.

worries.title: What worried you today?
worries.description: Copy over the worries you noted during the day. One sentence per worry.
worries.why: Postponing worries to a fixed time teaches you that you don't have to deal with them the moment they appear. Over time they take up less of your day.

stillMatters.title: How many still feel important?
stillMatters.description: Use the slider to mark what percentage of the noted worries still feels important now that you come back to them.
stillMatters.why: Many worries lose their weight within a few hours. Noticing this each evening weakens the belief that every one of them needs attention right away.

pick.title: Does any of them need action?
pick.description: If one of them is about a real problem you can influence, write down what needs doing. (Optional.)

followUp.title: Work the worry through in the tree
followUp.description: The worry tree helps separate a problem you can influence from a hypothetical you can let go of.

intro.title: Your anxiety map
intro.description: Anxiety is kept alive by avoidance and safety behaviours. They bring relief now but teach you the situation was dangerous. This map shows where to start.

situations.title: Which situations or topics make you anxious?
situations.description: Concrete situations, thoughts or images. They don't have to be big.

bodySigns.title: How does anxiety show in your body?
bodySigns.description: For example heart, breathing, stomach, tension, trembling.

avoidance.title: What do you avoid?
avoidance.description: Situations you put off, steer around or give up on.
avoidance.why: Avoidance brings relief right away but makes the anxiety stronger next time. This list is the material for facing it step by step.

safetyBehaviors.title: How do you keep yourself safe?
safetyBehaviors.description: Things you do to feel safer: checking, asking others for reassurance, over-preparing, holding your phone.
safetyBehaviors.why: Safety behaviours are quiet avoidance: when nothing bad happens, you credit them rather than yourself. So the anxiety doesn't fade.

cost.title: What do avoidance and safety behaviours cost you?
cost.description: What do you lose because of them: time, opportunities, relationships, energy?

title.m: What would you do if the anxiety were smaller?
title.f: What would you do if the anxiety were smaller?

withoutFear.description: One or two things you want to return to or start. (Optional.)
withoutFear.why: What anxiety keeps you from doing today shows where to head next. Facing anxiety is easier when you know what it is for.

keep.title: Which practices do you want to keep?
keep.description: Write up to three practices, each with how often you want to do it.
keep.why: Progress lasts better when a few practices stay in your weekly rhythm. A specific frequency turns an intention into a plan.

signal.title: How will you know it's time to come back?
signal.description: A concrete warning sign: an old reaction returning, more avoidance, a few worse weeks.
signal.why: Setbacks are normal. If you decide in advance how you'll recognise one, you'll get back to your practices before the old reaction settles in.

support.title: Who or what can help you with that?
support.description: A person, a reminder, a fixed time. (Optional.)
